Both countries consume beyond what autarky allowed

section: Where Does Comparative Advantage Come From?
text:
Where Does Comparative Advantage Come From?





Ricardian model (Ricardo, 1817)


Comparative advantage comes from differences in labor productivity — i.e., technology.
Countries specialize where their technology gives them an edge.
Key insight: technology, not endowments, drives the pattern.







Heckscher-Ohlin (H-O) model (early 20th c.)


Comparative advantage comes from factor endowments — the relative supply of capital, labor, land.

Capital-abundant countries → capital-intensive goods (autos, aircraft)
Labor-abundant countries → labor-intensive goods (apparel)

Key insight: who owns the abundant factor wins from trade.












Figure 4






Two workhorse models. Ricardo (early 19th c.) said comparative advantage comes from technology — Britain has better looms, so Britain makes cloth more productively than Portugal even if both have the same labor. Heckscher-Ohlin (early 20th c.) said it comes from factor endowments — Britain has more capital, so Britain specializes in capital-intensive goods, while Portugal with more labor specializes in labor-intensive goods. The bar chart below illustrates the H-O intuition with Oatley’s example: in auto manufacturing, labor is only about 25–30% of costs, with capital dominating; in apparel, labor takes the lion’s share. The H-O punchline is the one that matters most for political economy: the owners of the abundant factor gain from trade, while the owners of the scarce factor lose. In the U.S., that means capital-abundant industries (and capital owners) gain from trade; labor-abundant ones (and lower-skilled workers) lose. Hold onto that thought — this distributional asymmetry drives much of the politics of trade. We don’t need the full Stolper-Samuelson theorem today, but the intuition is: trade isn’t neutral within a country, even when it’s net-positive overall.

title: Global Development
text:
Trade Policy and Welfare
Standard introductory microeconomics. The left panel shows the welfare consequences of opening a closed economy to trade; the right panel shows how a tariff partially reverses them.








Figure 5








Opening to trade transfers area A from producers to consumers and creates area B as new welfare. A tariff partially reverses this: area A is transferred back to producers as new producer surplus, area C is collected by the government, and areas B and D are destroyed as deadweight loss.




This is the strongest economic argument for trade. Set up the small open economy: world price is below domestic autarky price; the country imports the difference. A tariff raises the domestic price above the world price. Producers respond by producing more (Q1 → Q2). Consumers respond by buying less (Q4 → Q3). Imports shrink. Government collects tariff revenue on what’s still imported (rectangle C). Now the welfare accounting: producers gain area A (their surplus increases because they get a higher price). Government collects area C (tariff revenue). But consumers lose A + B + C + D (their surplus falls by a much larger trapezoid). Net welfare change: gains are A + C; losses are A + B + C + D; net is −B − D. Areas B and D are pure deadweight loss — production we didn’t need at this cost, and consumption that doesn’t happen because the price is artificially high. This is the punchline: protection doesn’t transfer welfare from consumers to producers. It transfers some welfare to producers and government, AND destroys some welfare entirely. That’s why “free trade is good” isn’t just an ideological claim — it’s a welfare arithmetic claim.

title: Global Development
text:
What This Theory Assumes
The standard comparative-advantage argument rests on three contested assumptions:





Market clearing


Prices and wages adjust freely; labor markets clear; no persistent unemployment.
Trade adjustment costs in practice can persist for decades and remain geographically concentrated.







Constant or decreasing returns


Markets are competitive rather than oligopolistic.
Trade in aircraft, semiconductors, and software is dominated by a small number of firms operating under increasing returns to scale.







Neutral terms of trade


Relative prices do not systematically favor some producers over others.
The Prebisch-Singer hypothesis argues that commodity exporters face deteriorating terms of trade against manufactured-goods exporters.







The case for state intervention, in the next section, starts from the limits of these assumptions.




This is a signposting slide — flagging that the theory we just walked through makes assumptions that aren’t always true. Three big ones. (1) Market clearing: standard trade theory assumes prices and wages adjust to keep labor employed. In reality, the China Shock literature (Autor-Dorn-Hanson and others) shows that trade adjustment can be slow and geographically concentrated, with displaced workers not finding equivalent employment for years or decades. (2) Constant or decreasing returns to scale: the textbook story assumes competitive markets — many firms, no one with market power. Modern trade in aircraft, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, software is dominated by a small number of firms with massive economies of scale. That’s “new trade theory” (Krugman and others) — strategic interaction, market power, government intervention can shape who wins. Different politics, different policy implications. (3) Neutral terms of trade: the model assumes the relative prices of traded goods don’t systematically favor some producers. Prebisch and Singer argued in the 1950s that commodity exporters (developing countries) face deteriorating terms of trade against manufactured-goods exporters — a key intellectual foundation of import-substitution strategies in Latin America and elsewhere. The next section takes these up directly, since the case for intervention begins by relaxing them.

title: Global Development
text:
Distribution Within Countries



Distributional conflict over trade is both interstate and intrastate. Country-level accounts of “winners” and “losers” obscure the within-country coalitions that produce national trade positions.





Between countries
Some countries gain more from a given agreement than others. Bargaining power determines the distribution.

Within countries
Industries, regions, and factor owners gain and lose unevenly.
U.S. agriculture is heavily protected and subsidized despite farmers comprising roughly 1.5% of the population. The bicameral Senate gives Wyoming the same representation as California, amplifying the political power of rural producers.




“The U.S. position” in any negotiation is the position of the domestic coalition with sufficient political voice to define it.




This slide is critical and worth slowing down for. The standard trade-theory presentation talks about country-level gains and losses, which makes it sound like the political problem is just “U.S. vs. China” or “developed vs. developing.” But that’s only half of it. The other half — and arguably the more important half for politics — is within-country distribution. Even when comparative advantage says the U.S. gains overall, those gains go to some American workers, firms, and regions while other American workers, firms, and regions lose. The political question isn’t just “do we gain on net?” — it’s “which Americans gain, and which lose, and which group has more political power?” Big Ag is the clearest U.S. example. Farmers are tiny — about 1.5% of the population. But agriculture is one of the most heavily protected and most heavily subsidized sectors in the U.S. economy. Why? Because the bicameral system in the U.S. Senate gives each state two senators regardless of population, and farm-state senators wield enormous power over farm-state legislation. Wyoming (population 580,000) gets the same Senate representation as California (population 39 million). That structural feature of American political institutions massively amplifies the political power of rural producer interests. This is the society-centered view of trade politics (Stolper-Samuelson, coalitions, the Ricardo-Viner / specific-factors model), which the next section contrasts with a state-centered view. The point to make here: when we say “the U.S. position” in trade negotiations, we don’t mean some abstract national interest. We mean whichever domestic coalition has the political voice to define the U.S. position. That’s a much messier story than the textbook lets on.

title: Global Development
section: The State-Centered Approach: Two Core Claims
text:
The State-Centered Approach: Two Core Claims






Society-Centered


State-Centered






1 · Protection can RAISE welfare


Protection always destroys welfare — it forfeits the gains from trade and traps resources in losing industries.


Under specific conditions (scale, learning, rents), targeted intervention can move resources where the market won’t, increasing country-level aggregate welfare.




2 · The state can act ON ITS OWN


Policy is the outgrowth of interest-group pressure. The state has no goals of its own.


Under specific conditions, insulated policymakers pursue a national objective that no lobby asked for.








Both claims must hold jointly:

If protection cannot raise welfare, intervention is pointless.
If the state cannot act autonomously, the account reduces to society-centered lobbying.






The state-centered approach rests on two assumptions, and each one directly contradicts a pillar of the society-centered model. The first is a claim about welfare. The society-centered approach inherited the standard trade model’s verdict that protection is deadweight loss — it forfeits the gains from trade and keeps resources stuck in comparatively disadvantaged industries. The state-centered approach says: not always. Under a specific and limited set of conditions — economies of scale, learning effects, oligopoly rents — there are industries the market won’t move resources into even though society would gain in the long run, and a well-aimed intervention can correct that. The second assumption is about politics. The society-centered approach treats national policy as the resultant of interest-group forces. The state-centered approach says that under certain institutional conditions, policymakers are insulated enough to pursue an objective of their own — boosting a strategic industry, catching a rival, securing a supply — that no domestic lobby necessarily demanded. The crucial logical point for students: you need both assumptions together. If protection can never raise welfare, then autonomy just lets the state destroy value more efficiently. If the state can never act autonomously, then even a real welfare opportunity gets captured and distorted by whoever lobbies hardest. The rest of the lecture is essentially an examination of when — and whether — these two strong assumptions actually hold.

title: Global Development
section: Revisiting Core Assumptions - Market Failures Everywhere
text:
Revisiting Core Assumptions - Market Failures Everywhere
The gains-from-trade verdict — do not intervene — rests on the three contested assumptions from the previous section. The state-centered approach is favored by those who focus on the limits of those assumptions.




Assumption


What the free-trade case assumes


How the state-centered approach relaxes it →






Market clearing


Factors are allocated to their best use; no lasting unemployment — so a tariff can only destroy value.


Scale + learning curves strand factors below their long-run value — a social-vs-private return gap the market won’t close without public guidance.




Constant / decreasing returns


Markets are competitive: many firms, no market power.


High-tech runs on increasing returns and oligopoly. A few firms earn rents, and the country that hosts them captures the income.




Neutral terms of trade


Doesn’t really matter what goods you specialize in.


National wealth accrues when countries can move up the value chain. Staying stuck in primary production is bad for wealth and growth.







Relax perfect competition and constant returns and the case for free trade becomes more complicated and less absolute.




This slide connects the two halves of the lecture, and it’s worth making explicit because it shows that the case for intervention is not a separate topic — it is, in effect, the mirror image of the free-trade model from the first section. Go back to the “What This Theory Assumes” slide: it flagged three assumptions sitting behind the clean gains-from-trade result. Take them in order. One, market clearing: the standard model assumes factors glide to their highest-value use, which is precisely why a tariff could only ever block that movement and destroy value. The state-centered approach denies the premise — economies of scale and learning curves can strand resources below their long-run potential, opening a gap between social and private returns that the market won’t close on its own, and that gap is the entire welfare case for intervention we’re about to build. Two, constant or decreasing returns: the standard model assumed competition, many firms, nobody with market power. Drop that assumption and you land in the world of increasing returns and oligopoly, where a handful of firms earn rents and the country hosting them pockets the income. This is the “new trade theory” mentioned on the assumptions slide — Krugman’s world, and the basis of strategic-trade theory. Three, neutral terms of trade: relax the idea that no producer is systematically favored and you see that rents and first-mover advantages are contestable prizes a government can try to seize with a subsidy. The point to carry forward: every tool in the next section — infant-industry protection, subsidies, state-directed credit — depends on relaxing one or more of these three assumptions. That gives students a diagnostic they can use on any real-world intervention: ask which assumption the advocate is claiming fails here. If they can’t name one, the argument is probably interest-group politics described in the vocabulary of the national interest.

title: Global Development
text:
The Infant-Industry Case
A new industry may be unprofitable today but efficient tomorrow — if it survives long enough to grow up. Two mechanisms create that gap:


Economies of scale
Big fixed costs (an aircraft program ≈ $3B+). Unit cost falls only at high volume. A new entrant can’t reach that volume against incumbents who already have.

Economies of experience
Efficiency comes from doing — seasoned managers, skilled workers, reliable suppliers. The learning curve accrues through cumulative production; it cannot simply be purchased.




The argument has mercantilist roots: Alexander Hamilton (1791) and Friedrich List both sought tariffs to develop manufacturing against a dominant Britain — and the same argument was later applied to postwar Japan.




The economic core of the case for intervention is the infant-industry argument, and it is worth slowing down because every modern industrial-policy debate is a variation on it. The standard trade model rules out welfare-improving intervention by assumption: factors flow to their highest return, so a tariff only blocks that flow. To justify intervention you must identify something that stops factors from moving into an industry that would, in the long run, pay off. The classic answer is the infant industry — a firm not efficient initially but efficient eventually, if it is given time to mature. Two mechanisms generate that gap. Economies of scale: when fixed costs are enormous — Oatley’s example is a commercial aircraft program costing billions — unit costs fall only at high volume, but a newcomer can’t sell enough high-cost early output against established low-cost rivals to ever reach that volume. Economies of experience, or learning by doing: efficient production needs seasoned managers, skilled workers, and reliable suppliers, none of which exist in an infant industry by definition. Costs fall as you accumulate experience. The political pedigree matters: this is not a left-wing idea or a new idea. Alexander Hamilton made the argument in 1791 to build American manufacturing against British dominance; Friedrich List systematized it in Germany a half-century later; and many credit Japan’s postwar ascent to the same logic. Free-trade Britain was the incumbent; everyone climbing behind it reached for the tariff.

title: Global Development
text:
Climbing the Learning Curve








Figure 6








The newcomer’s dilemma: costs fall only with volume, but volume is unattainable while costs remain high. A temporary tariff or subsidy can solve this “low-level equilibrium trap” .




This figure makes the learning curve concrete and gives students something visual to remember. When Airbus assembled its very first fuselage it took roughly 340,000 person-hours. By the 75th aircraft that had fallen to about 85,000, and eventually to around 43,000. That improvement was not purchased; it was achieved through cumulative repetition — workers learning the job, managers refining the process, suppliers becoming reliable. Now see the trap. The newcomer is expensive precisely because it hasn’t yet produced much, and it can’t produce much because, being expensive, it can’t win customers away from incumbents who are already far down their own curve. Who buys the high-cost early output? In an open market, no one — so the firm never reaches the volume that would make it competitive. This is the welfare argument for a temporary intervention: guarantee the infant the domestic market for a while, let it produce enough to slide down the curve, and once it’s genuinely competitive, remove the protection. The phrase to underline is temporary. The entire welfare case depends on the tariff coming off once the industry grows up. Hold that thought, because the most serious real-world criticism of industrial policy is that the protection almost never comes off — the infant becomes a dependent adult with a powerful lobby.

title: Global Development
section: A Tariff Is Rarely the Best Tool
text:
A Tariff Is Rarely the Best Tool








Figure 7








The economists’ rule: target the actual distortion.

A profitable-but-cash-starved firm should borrow — and if financing is the binding constraint, the government can subsidize the borrowing itself (a loan or guarantee), not the output.
A skills-spillover problem needs workforce training, not a tariff.
Intervention is justified only where a real market failure creates a major coordination problem (government needs to make both the demand and supply side of the market).





This slide is Oatley’s “A Closer Look” box, and it teaches students how an economist actually reasons about intervention — by asking what specific market failure you’re correcting and choosing the narrowest tool that fixes it. Start at the left. A tariff helps the infant, but it does so by taxing domestic consumers, who now pay more — a real welfare loss. So move right: a subsidy delivers the same help to the firm without gouging consumers, which is why economists prefer it to a tariff. But now comes the sharper objection, and it applies to subsidies too. If a firm really will be profitable in the long run, it should be able to borrow against those future profits in private capital markets to cover its early losses. If it can borrow, it doesn’t need the government. And if it can’t borrow — if private investors, looking at the same future, decline to fund it — then the market is telling you this isn’t society’s best use of scarce capital, so the government shouldn’t fund it either. That argument is the free-market case against industrial policy in compressed form. It fails in exactly two circumstances, and they’re worth memorizing because they define the legitimate zone for intervention. One: the payoff comes from training workers who can then quit and take their skills to rivals, so no single firm can capture the return — a classic spillover, best fixed by broad training programs, not firm subsidies. Two: the capital market itself is broken and won’t lend to good projects — in which case the first-best fix is to repair the capital market, not to subsidize the firm. The through-line: intervention is defensible only where you can name a real market failure that blocks the private borrowing solution.

title: Global Development
section: State Strength: Who Can Actually Do This?
text:
State Strength: Who Can Actually Do This?
Industrial policy = tax breaks, subsidies and state credit, protection, and procurement, used to steer resources toward favored industries.
Whether a state can do so depends on state strength — how insulated policymakers are from interest groups.




State


Institutions & track record


Insulation






Japan — STRONG


Centralized authority; MITI/METI + Ministry of Finance coordinate. “Administrative guidance” steered capital from heavy industry (1950s) to high-tech (1970s).


High




France — STRONG


Insulated bureaucracy; “National Champions” strategy. Backed Renault, steel — and a national computer firm (Machines Bull) that flopped.


High




United States — WEAK


Federalism + divided powers + porous agencies → captured easily. Yet runs a de facto industrial policy through DEFENSE: R&D, procurement, the internet, early chips.


Low (but the Pentagon is a loophole)







Strength cuts both ways. Insulation lets a state plan for the long run and pull protection once the infant matures — but it also removes the check that stops the state from picking badly.




Now we connect the economics to institutions, because even if intervention can work in theory, only some states are equipped to implement it. First, the definition: industrial policy is the use of a broad toolkit — tax policy, subsidies including state-directed credit, traditional protection, and government procurement — to channel resources away from some industries and toward those the state wants to grow. The capacity to wield that toolkit coherently is what Oatley calls state strength: the degree to which policymakers are insulated from interest-group pressure. Strong states centralize authority, coordinate across agencies, and offer few access points to lobbyists. Japan is the textbook strong state — MITI, now METI, working with the Ministry of Finance, used “administrative guidance” to move capital from steel and shipbuilding in the early postwar years into high-technology in the 1970s, and many credit this for the Japanese miracle. France is the other strong-state case, with its insulated bureaucracy and its “National Champions” strategy — though notice Oatley’s honest detail that the French national computer champion, Machines Bull, failed to become competitive, an early reminder that strength guarantees coherence, not success. The United States is the canonical weak state: federalism, separated powers, and porous agencies create so many channels for lobbying that officials struggle to act coherently in any “national interest.” And yet — this is the move I want students to catch — the U.S. runs a large de facto industrial policy through the back door of national defense: Pentagon R&D and procurement underwrote computing, the internet, and the early semiconductor industry. That defense loophole is the historical seed of today’s “economic security” turn. Last point, and it’s the double edge: insulation is exactly what lets a strong state plan long-term and, crucially, withdraw protection once an industry matures — but it’s also what removes the feedback that would tell the state it has chosen badly. Strength is not the same as good judgment.

title: Global Development

What this course is
INTL-522 is a core course for the MA in International Studies and a core requirement for the Global Development, Environment, and Sustainability concentration in the MIA.
We address large questions:

Why are some countries poor while others are not?
What theories explain the divergence, and how would we know whether one of them were right?
What regularities show up in the historical record of rising standards of living, and what have been the consequences?

We do this to develop a set of competing accounts of how development (an extraordinarily complex process) happens, evaluate these accounts against evidence, assemble our own working “theory of change,” and assess what kinds of approaches to development as a project are more or less likely to have positive outcomes.

A toolkit for project management, monitoring, or evaluation
A regional survey
Primarily an interpretive critique of development

section: What do we mean when we talk about Development?
text:
What do we mean when we talk about Development?


Outcome

A state of affairs at a point in time: income, health, schooling, what people are actually able to do.
This is measurable and comparable across countries, but doesn’t explain why countries are at a particular level of development.


Process

Structural transformation over time — sectoral shift, urbanization, demographic transition, the slow accumulation of state capacity.
Explanation for why, when, and how this change occurs.


Project

A deliberate intervention by actors who claim the authority to direct someone else’s trajectory.
Requires actors to undertake the project (design, bankrolling, implementation)
Generates politics

title: Global Development
text:
How are we approaching development?
A claim like “development failed in Africa” might mean that outcomes are bad, or that the transformation stalled, or that the interventions did not work. Those are three separate claims, and I’ve designed this course to help you interrogate each of them.
The six books we will read all address different components of development:

Sen conceptualizes development to help us measure it better. You can’t do this without making a series of normative judgments!
Koyama & Rubin provide the most comprehensive, synthetic, historical view of what lead to the divergence in development trajectories across “the West” and late industrializers.
Evans is a canonical treatment of when states can effectively speed up development processes.
Cramer, Sender & Oqubay provide a sustained look at Africa and present a heterodox approach to what the development as a project community has gotten wrong there.
Kentikelenis & Stubbs look at how attempts by key international development organizations (IMF/World Bank) to guide development have fared
Banerjee & Duflo shift the focus from macroeconomies to households and consider how smaller scale interventions can sum to broader development trajectories.

title: Global Development
text:
Economic development and human development
Growth in output per person and expansion in what people are able to do and be are related, but they are not equivalent.

Income purchases some capabilities more reliably than others
Two countries at similar income levels can differ substantially in life expectancy, schooling, and freedom from arbitrary power
Income is distributed unevenly within countries, and even within families

Sen’s contribution is to move beyond utilitarian conceptions of aggregate welfare and libertarian conceptions of absolute politicla freedom to instead think of income as one component of capabilities and how we might go about measuring development from a capabilities rather than income perspective
Keep that in mind through the measures we are about to look at, most of which are built on income.

Extreme poverty over three decades


June 2025: the World Bank changed the threshold for extreme poverty from $2.15/day (2017 PPP) to $3.00/day (2021 PPP)
Same year, same household surveys: 713 million below the old line, 838 million below the new


847 million people below the line in 2024. The decline is one of the largest changes in human welfare on record and is concentrated in East and South Asia. It has slowed, and extreme poverty rose in 2020 by roughly 71 million, the first increase since 1998.

15% of world population, 50% of the extreme poor

UNHCR counted 117.8 million forcibly displaced at the end of 2025, down 4% on large-scale returns to Afghanistan, Syria, and Sudan — the first decline in a decade.

section: Two kinds of inequality, moving in opposite directions
text:
Two kinds of inequality, moving in opposite directions


1820: nearly all global inequality is within countries, because nearly everywhere is poor. Industrialization opens a between-country gap peaking around 1980 at 57% of the total. Since then China and India close much of it while inequality inside countries rises, putting within-country back to 68% by 2020. Between-country convergence stalled around 2015 and reversed in 2020 — anything past 2020 is projection.

Geometric mean of health, education, income
Global HDI 0.756; inequality-adjusted 0.590, so 22% is lost to distribution
2024’s projected increase is the smallest since 1990

The vintage problem, if it comes up: HDR 2021/22 reported two consecutive global declines in 2020 and 2021, the first on record, with over 90% of countries falling in one of those years. HDR 2025’s revised back-series shows both years flat at 0.742. Both are accurate — UNDP rebuilds the whole historical series each year as inputs are revised. Worth raising when they ask which HDR to cite.

Excluded from chart - The Multidimensional Poverty Index, counts deprivations directly: 1.1 billion people, 18.3% of the 6.3 billion it covers

One point per country; dashed line = the two measures agree

Regional banks: ADB around $40B, IDB $23.4B, EBRD €16.6B, AfDB $11B

The 2025 contraction in development finance

USAID: stop-work order January 2025, dissolved into State on July 1, over 80% of programs terminated
US foreign assistance: $73.5B (FY24) → $47.3B (FY25), down 35.6%, lowest since 2004
DAC ODA: down 23.1% in real terms to $174.3B — the largest annual decline on record
Donor giving now 0.26% of combined GNI
Cuts: US −56.9% · Germany −17.4% · France −10.9% · UK −10.8%
Still meeting 0.7%: Norway, Luxembourg, Sweden, Denmark


Say plainly that they are entering the field at a moment when its financing model has changed and nobody knows the new steady state. This returns when we reach Kentikelenis and Stubbs.

Development is a complex system: many causes, long lags, two-way feedback, non-exchangeable units
Identification is hard, and development is likely contingent
Every intervention still rest on a theory (or “theory of change”) — loan conditions, cash transfers, industrial policy
Left implicit, that theory goes untested
Making it explicit, then testing it against evidence, can improve intervention


The failure mode to correct if the room drifts there: difficulty is a reason to be careful about what we claim, not a reason to stop asking.

title: Course Précis
text: Throughout the semester, you will work individually and as a collective to develop a synthetic overview of the key concepts of this course — a high-quality summary of the material that you can take with you when the semester ends. This is the course précis. It is the one assignment whose primary audience is your future self: done well, it is the document you will reach for years from now when you need to remember how the pieces of the development literature fit together. This page provides detailed instructions; the assignments page has the summary and the syllabus has grade weights and policies.

title: Course Précis
text:
What it is
The précis is a combination of words and figures. We will especially think about causal chains — what causes development, through what mechanisms, on what evidence — so your document must include these chains as diagrams, not only as prose. A reader should be able to look at your figures and see your understanding of how geography, institutions, states, markets, international forces, and household behavior connect to development outcomes, and where the major theories disagree about those connections.
There is no fixed page length. Most strong précis documents end up somewhere around 6–10 pages including figures, but I will evaluate synthesis, not volume. A tight document that maps the arguments accurately beats a long one that summarizes each book in sequence.

title: Course Précis
section: How it builds across the semester
text:
How it builds across the semester
The précis is not a document you write at the end; it is a document you revise all term. The course is structured to help you develop a habit of consistently revising and updating it:

Your session notes are the raw material. Every Part 1 entry states a reading’s central causal claim — those claims are the nodes and arrows of your map. The Connector role does précis work explicitly: each week, the Connector’s additions help revise and update the shared causal map we develop together in class, and that shared map informs (but does not replace) each student’s individual document. Therefore, everyone in the class will be better off if the Connector for the week takes their role seriously and shares their notes with the group. The Discussion Leaders should be sure to structure class conversation to ensure that there is ample discussion on connections across weeks. The better your session notes as well as the notes you take during class discussion, the easier time you’ll have constructing your course précis.
The Oct 12 workshop is the first checkpoint. Bring a working draft that maps the causal arguments of Sen, Koyama & Rubin, and Evans against each other. We will spend the session comparing maps, arguing about where the arrows go, and identifying what each framework treats as the binding constraint on development. Your draft can be rough — hand-drawn figures are welcome at this stage — but you must do the pre-work; the class session will not be helpful if you show up unprepared.
Each new book complicates the map. After the Africa book, A Thousand Cuts, Poor Economics, and the AI unit, expect to revise: some causal arrows will see their evidence strengthen, some causal pathways may seem to diminish, and some of what looked like settled understanding of what causes development in September will no longer seem so straightforward in November. Tracking those revisions is the intellectual point of the assignment.

I evaluate the précis on the accuracy with which it represents the arguments we studied, the quality of the synthesis across books (connections and adjudication, not book-by-book summary), the clarity and correctness of the causal diagrams, and its usefulness as a standalone document — could a strong student entering this course next year learn the terrain from your précis? Figures may be drawn in any tool you like, or drawn by hand and scanned cleanly.

title: Session Notes & Discussion Roles
text: Session notes are the core way that students meaningfully prepare for each meeting of this seminar. Every member writes before every class that has assigned reading, everyone’s writing is used in the room, and each of you has a different job for discussion each week. This page provides detailed instructions for this set of assignments; the assignments page has the summary and the syllabus has grade weights and policies.

title: Session Notes & Discussion Roles
text:
The note
Bring five printed copies of your structured session notes to class — one for me, and one for each of you. Each note has two parts.

Part 1 — the core (200–300 words, everyone)
Answer three questions about the day’s reading:

The claim. What is the reading’s central causal claim about development? State it in your own words, as precisely as you can — what causes what, through what mechanism?
The evidence. What evidence does the author offer, and does it convince you? Name the kind of evidence (historical narrative, cross-country comparison, case study, experiment) and say where it is strongest and weakest.
Your argument. One point you are prepared to argue in class — a disagreement with the author, an extension, or a tension with something we read earlier.



Part 2 — your role (100–150 words)
Each week you hold one of four roles, and your note adds a short section written from that role’s perspective:


 Discussion Leader
Develop a set of 3–5 discussion questions that you think are most central to understanding and evaluating the reading. Good discussion questions move progressively from concrete to interpretive and from narrow to wide. Next to each question, provide a sentence on why this question matters. In class, you open the discussion and keep it moving — when a thread exhausts itself, you bring us to the next question. I, as the instructor, will help to keep the conversation moving productively and can assist students with decoding any questions that arise from the reading. Note that in many class sessions I will have a short set of slides to present to help ground the discussion in a clear narrative arc that is informed by the structure of international development as an academic discipline.


 Skeptic
Interrogate the evidence. Identify the weakest link in the causal chain: an alternative explanation the author hasn’t ruled out, a measurement or design problem, a case that doesn’t fit. In class, you make the strongest version of the counterargument — even if you personally find the author convincing.


 Connector
Tie the reading to the rest of the course. Where does it agree, conflict, or fill a gap relative to earlier books and articles? What would this author say to one we’ve already read? In class, you will bring in these comparisons — and your connections will help revise and update the shared causal map we will develop throughout the semester to inform each student’s course précis.


 Practitioner
Translate the argument into practice. If this author is right, what should a government, international organization, NGO, or firm do differently? What would the argument’s policy implications cost, and who would resist them? In class, you ground the discussion in application.

title: Session Notes & Discussion Roles
text:
Rotation
Roles are assigned in week 1 and rotate weekly, so you hold each role for a full week (both sessions) and cycle through all four roughly every four weeks — about three turns in each role across the semester. The rotation schedule is posted on Canvas alongside the Data Project 1 region sign-up sheet.

title: Session Notes & Discussion Roles
text:
How notes get used
We open most sessions with a short slide-based lecture from me. This will anchor our discussion to broader ideas, claims, and debates in the academic and practitioner community. Then, we will lay out the four Part 1 claims side by side, and you will each have a few minutes to write down any observations that arise from reading your peers’ responses next to yours. Where your readings of the book diverge is where discussion starts — divergence is material to explore, not an indication that someone made an error of interpretation. The Discussion Leader’s agenda structures the rest of the hour, the Skeptic and Connector give the discussion its friction and its memory, and the Practitioner keeps us honest about stakes. Nothing you write is filed away unread; all of it does work in the room.
Save everything: your Part 1 claims and the Connector work in particular will be important as you develop your course précis.

Logistics and grading

Length: 300–450 words total (200–300 core + 100–150 role). The word limits are real and I will enforce them. Being able to distill your thoughts is part of the skill you are developing through this assignment.
Due: on paper at the start of class. Late notes receive no credit (the class needs them before discussion).
Grading: credit/no-credit. Roughly 21 sessions require notes; your best 18 count, so you can miss or fumble a few without a grade penalty.

About This Course
I-522 is a core graduate course for the Masters of International Studies and a core requirement for the Global Development, Environment, and Sustainability concentration of the Masters of International Affairs. We take on large questions: Why are some countries poor while others are not? What theories and approaches explain this divergence? We examine the political, economic, social, and cultural forces shaping development outcomes, and we consider the roles of geography, institutions, markets, states, international organizations, and domestic governance along the way.
This is a seminar; lecture is minimal. The course works through sustained discussion of six books and a set of recent articles, and it depends on every member arriving prepared, every session. In a small seminar, your preparation is not private — it is the raw material the class runs on.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course description
INTL-I 522 Theoretical and Empirical Overview of Global Development (3 cr.) Explores theories and approaches of global development as well as the political, economic, social, and cultural forces shaping global development outcomes. Considers the role of geography, institutions, global markets and trade, civil society, and historical forces in exploration of the causes and consequences of development.
I-522 is a core graduate course for the Masters of International Studies and a core requirement for the Global Development, Environment, and Sustainability concentration of the Masters of International Affairs. We take on large questions: Why are some countries poor while others are not? What are the principal theories and approaches that explain this divergence? What are the empirical regularities — drivers and consequences — of increased standards of living? We work through six books and a set of recent articles that together trace the field’s central debates, from the meaning and measurement of development itself, through the historical origins of modern growth, the role of the state in industrial transformation, the political economy of Africa’s development, the international institutions that discipline poor-country policy, and the micro-level economics of poverty — ending with the newest frontier: what AI may mean for development. There are no graduate-level prerequisites for this class.

title: Syllabus
text:
Aims & outcomes
By the end of this course you will be able to:

Explain and critically compare the major theoretical approaches to global development — capabilities, institutionalist, structuralist, and experimental — and identify what each takes to be the binding constraint on development.
Evaluate the empirical evidence behind competing causal claims about development, including the strengths and limits of cross-country, historical, and experimental research designs.
Analyze how development is measured, what different measures capture and conceal, and how measurement choices shape policy — at both macro and household levels, using real data.
Assess the role of international institutions, markets, and geopolitics in enabling and constraining development strategies.
Construct your own synthetic causal map of development — the course précis — and defend it.
Produce professional-genre analysis: a policy memo or synthetic literature review, developed through structured milestones and presented to peers.

Course policies

Intellectual diversity
Development is a field of live disagreement — about what causes growth, what states should do, and what rich countries owe poor ones. Course materials present a variety of arguments, and the seminar is designed for thoughtful, reasoned debate. Four rules help:

Frame disagreements as debates rather than conflicts.
Argue as if you are right, but listen as if you are wrong.
Make the most respectful interpretation of the other person’s perspective.
Acknowledge where you agree with others and what you’ve learned from peers with whom you differ.



Generative AI policy
Generative AI tools are now part of research and policy work, and you may use them in this course — within limits, under your supervision, and with full disclosure.

As a research tool. You may use AI to help you locate literature, explore data, summarize material, and test your understanding of the readings. You are responsible for verifying everything an AI tells you against the actual sources. These tools fabricate citations and misstate findings with complete confidence; an invented source or a wrong claim in your work is your error, not the tool’s.
As a writing aid — supervised and heavily revised. You may use AI to help with some of your writing. Any AI-assisted text must be heavily edited and revised by you before it appears in your work. You are responsible for the precision of your prose and for keeping the common markers of AI writing from overwhelming it: “it’s not X, it’s Y” constructions, overconfident assertion, strange word choices, and a generic voice that is not your own. If a passage reads like a chatbot wrote it, you have not finished the assignment.
Disclosure, always. Every submission in which you used AI in any way — for research, data work, or writing — must include a brief AI-use note stating which tools you used and for what. Undisclosed AI use is academic misconduct and will be handled under the Code of Student Rights, Responsibilities, and Conduct.
The exception: session notes. Session notes must be written entirely in your own words, without generative AI. They are your discussion preparation — your thinking made visible — and the gap between what you wrote and what you can say in the room is immediately obvious.

If you are ever unsure whether a particular use is permitted, ask first.


Accommodations for religious observances
IU respects the right of all students to observe their religion. If you require accommodations for a religious observance, submit a request by the end of the second week (a separate request per absence). I will approve these provided they’re filed within the first two weeks, and you’ll have an opportunity to make up missed work.


Email & office hours
Reserve email for clarifying questions or scheduling; office hours are for substantive questions and grade discussions. I try to respond within one business day. Office hours are also a chance for me to get to know you — which works to your advantage (I write much better recommendation letters for students I know). Arrive with specific questions.


Re-grading requests
After graded material is returned, I maintain a 48-hour reflection period before discussing grades. When I re-examine work with fresh eyes, I reserve the right to assign a grade lower than the original if appropriate.


Honor code
As an IU student you are expected to adhere to the Code of Student Rights, Responsibilities, and Conduct. Submitting work with your name on it signifies it is yours unless otherwise cited. Suspected violations are handled per University policy and reported to the Dean of Students.

title: Final Project
text: The final project is where you take ownership of one development question and produce something in a professional genre — the kind of document you may write in your career. It is an individual project, developed across the second half of the semester through a series of milestones, presented to the class in our final week, and revised before final submission. This page provides detailed instructions; the assignments page has the summary and the syllabus has grade weights and policies.

title: Final Project
text:
Choosing your genre
You will choose one of two genres. Both are legitimate professional forms, and the right choice depends on your interests and career goals. I encourage you to come to office hours before the topic memo is due to talk through your options.

 Option 1 — Policy memo
A memo of no more than 4 pages, single-spaced (plus appendices), addressed to a specific government agency, international organization, or NGO of your choice. Your memo will analyze one development challenge and propose a course of action. Do not let the short length fool you: memos must be impeccably researched, and it will be hard to cover everything you need in that little space. The discipline of deciding what to leave out is a large part of what this genre teaches. This option will help you develop the capacity to translate research into potential policy strategies.


 Option 2 — Synthetic literature review
A review of 10–15 pages, single-spaced, providing an authoritative overview of the main concepts, findings, and debates around one question of development. This is a deep dive into an issue we covered briefly in class, or one we did not cover at all. Your review should organize the literature around its debates rather than marching through papers one at a time, evaluate the kinds of evidence scholars use to assess theoretical claims, and offer suggestions for how the literature could move forward. This option is especially useful if you are considering a PhD or a more research-oriented (rather than policy or practitioner) trajectory.

title: Final Project
text:
What makes a strong project
Whichever genre you choose, I will be looking for the same underlying qualities we practice all semester in session notes: a precisely stated causal claim, intellectually honest engagement with the evidence for and against it (rather than relying on motivated reasoning), and awareness of what the argument implies for practice. Strong projects take a position. A memo that lists considerations without recommending anything, or a literature review that summarizes extant research without adjudicating persistent debates in the field, has not finished the analytic work.
Your topic should connect to the themes of this course, but it does not need to come from the assigned readings. If you are unsure whether a topic will work, ask early.

title: Data Projects
text:
You will complete two data projects during this semester — one at the macro and one at the micro level.
In the first, you look at development from above — the aggregate measures that governments, international organizations, and scholars use to say whether a country is developing.
In the second, you look from below — household-level data on how poor families actually earn, spend, borrow, and manage risk.
These projects, then, function in part to help us address a question of levels in development. How do individual behaviors aggregate to economy-wide progress on a range of development measures? Is development an individualistic/household project or a social one?
These are data literacy projects, not statistics projects. I am not asking you to run regressions, and you do not need any statistical training beyond careful reading of charts and tables. The skills being practiced here are the ones you will use constantly in policy careers: finding credible data, understanding what a measure actually captures, presenting numbers in an unbiased way, and drawing conclusions that the data can support.

title: Data Projects
text:
Data Project 1 — Measuring Development

Assigned Mon Aug 31 · Due Friday Sep 4 by COB, on Canvas · 7.5%

How development is measured shapes what development means — this is one of Sen’s central points, and this project helps you see this in practice by comparing different measures of development.

The task

Choose a region (Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, Latin America, Southeast Asia, MENA, or Central Asia), and within it, three focus countries with different development trajectories. Each student should take a different region — coordinate on the sign-up sheet posted on Canvas.
Choose at least three distinct measures of development. At least one must be income-based (GDP per capita, ideally PPP-adjusted; or the international poverty headcount) and at least one must be non-income or composite (HDI, the Multidimensional Poverty Index, inequality-adjusted HDI, life expectancy, mean years of schooling). The resources page lists where you can find each of these data sources.
Chart the trends. For each measure, show how your focus countries have moved over the longest sensible window the data allow (for GDP per capita that may be 60 years; for the MPI it may be 15 — and that difference in coverage is itself worth discussing). Every figure needs labeled axes, units, years, and a source line.
Analyze what the measures capture and hide. Where do your measures agree about which country is doing well, and where do they disagree? What does each measure assume development is? What would Sen say about each? Which countries look different depending on the yardstick — and why, concretely?
Take a position. Close with a short recommendation: if you could report only one of your measures to a minister or country director to track this region’s progress, which would you choose, and what would you be knowingly giving up?



The deliverable
A data brief of 3–4 pages (single-spaced, figures included in the page count), written for an intelligent professional reader, plus a data appendix (not counted in the page limit) listing every series you used: indicator name, source, years covered, and any gaps or oddities you encountered. Submit as a PDF on Canvas by COB Sept 4, and come to class on Sept 9 ready to present your findings in about five minutes at the debrief — expect questions about why the measures disagree.

title: Data Projects
section: Data Project 2 — The Economic Lives of the Poor
text:
Data Project 2 — The Economic Lives of the Poor

Assigned week of Nov 16 · Due Fri Nov 20, COB; on Canvas · presented at the Nov 30 debrief · 7.5%

Banerjee and Duflo’s Poor Economics emphasizes a different level of analysis: instead of asking how poor countries behave, they ask how poor households behave. This project has you explore this microlevel of analysis with real household data — and then confront what you find with the macroeconomic picture you built in Project 1.

The task

Choose one country — ideally, one of your three focus countries from Project 1, so the macro–micro comparison is direct. (If you switch countries, say why in the brief.)
Build a portrait of poor households’ economic lives in that country, covering three of these five domains, with at least six indicators total:

Earning: income sources, informality, agricultural vs. non-farm work
Spending: budget shares, food vs. non-food, spending that surprises you
Financial lives: saving, borrowing, account ownership (Global Findex is built for this)
Risk: health shocks, insurance coverage, coping strategies
Investing in the future: education and health spending, school enrollment and attainment

Use household-level sources. DHS STATcompiler, Global Findex, LSMS tables, IPUMS tabulations, or a J-PAL evaluation’s published data — the resources page links each. These tools give you tabulated indicators; you do not need to analyze or manipulate raw survey microdata (though you may).
Confront the two levels. Where does the household view confirm what Banerjee and Duflo report, and where does your country diverge from their composite picture of “the poor”? Most importantly: what does the micro view reveal that your Project 1 aggregates concealed — and is there anything the aggregates showed that the household data cannot?



The deliverable
Same format as Project 1: a 3–4 page data brief with a data appendix, submitted as a PDF on Canvas by Friday, Nov 20 at COB, and a roughly five-minute presentation at the Nov 30 debrief.
